strengths: DDOME targets a useful capability: selecting a small expert subset for an unseen client using unlabeled inputs, without local fine-tuning. Combining client-level expert selection with per-example routing is a practical design.

Experiments cover four image/text datasets, two forms of label heterogeneity, and ablations on anchors, pretraining, initialization, and changing client populations. Reported improvements over the common expert on CIFAR100 (73% to 78.6%) and Yahoo! Answers (69% to 74.9%) are promising.

The main training protocol is understandable from the objectives and pseudocode. The paper candidly reports failure cases and dependence on pretraining and anchor sampling, and acknowledges fairness risks. No material ethical concern is apparent in the benchmark study.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as stated. Under x ~ N(0, I_d/√d), take m=2. Unit-norm ground-truth experts imply E[y²] ≤ 2/√d, so the zero predictor has loss ≤ 1/√d. The two exact minimizations in equations (1)-(2) cannot increase this bound, contradicting the claimed dimension-independent Ω(1) loss. Appendix J also invokes a small-projection bound between W* and span(V,V*) despite allowing W*=V*, which invalidates that step. These are substantive problems with the central theoretical contribution.

Even a corrected theorem would address only one procedure: fitting experts under a frozen random router, then fitting the router with frozen experts. Failure of this procedure does not establish the general necessity of joint training. There is also no controlled empirical comparison of joint training against frozen-router or sequential alternatives.

The evidence does not isolate specialization arising from implicit heterogeneity. Appendix A explicitly constructs disjoint label groups for quantity-based anchors; these anchors receive fixed expert assignments, supervise the router with expert-ID targets, and occupy half the participating clients per round. The overlapping-label Dirichlet experiment is useful, but comparisons against simpler anchor-trained specialists and direct routing/specialization diagnostics are needed to distinguish learned structure from supplied grouping.

Baseline behavior substantially weakens the headline comparisons. With the 93% CIFAR10 checkpoint, FedAvg falls to 58.4% and FedMix to 42.9%, while SCAFFOLD collapses. Appendix B explicitly identifies learning-rate incompatibility as one explanation, and text optimization schedules differ across methods without a documented tuning protocol. The approximately 24-point headline gain should be contextualized against the frozen checkpoint, over which DDOME gains 2.7 points. Appendix G's matched-expert experiment helps but does not resolve these concerns across the main evaluation.

Originality relative to mixture-based personalized federated learning is insufficiently established. Joint MoE training is already standard, and comparisons largely emphasize global-model baselines beyond FedMix. Appendix I's K-means visualization does not substantiate the broad dismissal of clustering or mixture approaches for heterogeneous client distributions.

Reproducibility and statistical support are incomplete. The manuscript provides no code link or exact common-expert checkpoints/pretraining recipe despite strong sensitivity to their quality; router width and the text learning-rate decay factor are also unspecified. Run counts and uncertainty estimates are absent. Tables 7-8 report the best test accuracy during training without describing validation-based checkpoint selection.

Efficiency claims lack quantitative validation. There are no end-to-end communication-byte, latency, memory, or compute comparisons accounting for the common feature extractor and expert models. The main comparisons use two transmitted experts for both DDOME and FedMix while differing in total expert capacity, so they do not directly establish the claimed communication–accuracy advantage.
